title: Greet by name
promptHtml:
Write a method greet that takes a name and returns a greeting.

greet("Ada") must return exactly Hello, Ada! — capital H, a comma, one space, then the name, then an exclamation mark. An empty name is still a name: greet("") returns Hello, !.

You are writing a method, not a program. There is no main here — the checks below are run for you.
hints:
Two strings are joined with +. The result is a new string; neither original is changed.

Build the whole thing in one expression: something before the name, something after it.

"Hello, " + name + "!" — mind the space after the comma.
solutionNotesHtml:
+ between strings is the one operator in Java that is overloaded, and it is overloaded by the language rather than by anything you can write yourself.

What the compiler actually generates here is not a chain of concatenations. As of Java 9 it emits a single invokedynamic instruction that hands the pieces to a bootstrap method, which builds a formatter once and reuses it. You can see that for yourself: the bytecode of any string concatenation shows makeConcatWithConstants rather than a series of StringBuilder.append calls.

That matters later, in the loop chapter, where the distinction between one concatenation and a concatenation per iteration is the difference between a linear program and a quadratic one. One + is free. A += inside a loop is not.
